newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sets minimum prices on D-RAM chips.
newsitem.headline: EU sets minimum prices on D-RAM chips.

text.p: The European Commission said Monday it was introducing minimum prices on D-RAM computer chips originating in Japan and South Korea, effective immediately, although in reality prices will rise only next month.
The decision caught all sides of the industry unaware -- and nobody seemed happy with it.

European manufacturers of dynamic random access memory chips said the move does not go far enough to protect the fragile market, computer makers were angered that they cannot buy the cheapest available, and consumers will pay for the affair at stores throughout the EU.
The measures are intended to protect EU producers of D-RAMs that include Motorola Inc., Siemens AG and Texas Instruments Inc., said a European Commission official.
"It is a classic no-win situation," the official said. "You could see this one coming from a long way off."
The EU imposed anti-dumping duties on Japanese exporters in January 1990 and later on South Korean exporters, but the measures were suspended 21 months ago because D-RAM prices were rising.
But there is now a glut of D-RAM chips -- used in products ranging from mobile telephones to computers -- and the EU has decided to re-introduce protection measures.

The move follows complaints from European chip producers who have accused their South Korean and Japanese counterparts of selling chip products at below manufacturing cost in Europe in order to protect market share.
The EU market for D-RAM chips was worth $5.7 billion in 1995, a Commission official said, of which South Korean and Japanese manufacturers have over 60 percent.
